parts: Food is any substance that yields energy, builds new cells, repairs tissues and aids production of useful body compounds. Food groups: energy-giving foods (carbohydrates and fats: cereals, sugar, jaggery, oils), body-building foods (proteins: pulses, milk, egg, meat, fish) and protective or regulatory foods (minerals, vitamins, roughage, water: green leafy vegetables, fruits, amla, guava). Nutrition is the sum of the processes by which an organism takes in, metabolises and uses food. Nutrients are macronutrients (carbohydrates, fats, proteins, water) and micronutrients (vitamins and minerals).

Carbohydrates (C, H, O): the cheapest source of energy, 60-80 per cent of the energy in the diet; 1 g gives about 17-18 kJ (4 kcal); 1 kcal = 4.18 kJ; sugars (glucose, fructose, sucrose, lactose, maltose), starch (storage form; cereals, potato) and cellulose (roughage). Functions: energy (glucose is the only source of energy for the nervous system), excess stored as glycogen and fat, lactose helps absorption of calcium, cellulose gives faecal bulk. Fats (triglycerides): richest energy source, 1 g gives about 9 kcal (37 kJ); sources: ghee, butter, oils, nuts; functions: energy, structural component of membranes, absorption of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K, precursor of hormones, insulation (subcutaneous fat) and padding of vital organs. Proteins (C, H, O, N, sometimes P and S): polymers of amino acids; 1 g gives about 4 kcal; essential amino acids (not made by the body, e.g. leucine) and non-essential amino acids (alanine); sources: milk, egg, fish, meat, pulses, cereals (dal-roti combinations give all the essential amino acids); functions: growth, repair, enzymes, hormones (insulin), antibodies, transport (haemoglobin), structural proteins (keratin, collagen) and contractile proteins (actin, myosin).

Vitamins: organic compounds needed in tiny amounts that act as biocatalysts; water-soluble (B complex and C) and fat-soluble (A, D, E, K). Vitamin A (retinol): vision; deficiency causes night blindness and xerophthalmia; sources: carrot, mango, papaya, milk, liver. B1 (thiamine): beri-beri. B2 (riboflavin): cracking of the skin at the corners of the mouth. B3 (niacin): pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia). B12 (cyanocobalamin): pernicious anaemia. C (ascorbic acid): scurvy (bleeding gums, joint pain); amla, citrus, guava. D (calciferol): rickets in children (bow legs, pigeon chest) and osteomalacia in adults; made in skin in sunlight; cod liver oil, egg yolk. E (tocopherol): sterility, miscarriage. K: delayed blood clotting.

Minerals: calcium and phosphorus (bones and teeth; deficiency causes rickets and osteomalacia; osteoporosis in the elderly makes bones fragile), iron (haemoglobin; deficiency causes anaemia: paleness, tiredness, loss of weight, low haemoglobin), iodine (thyroxine; deficiency causes goitre; iodised salt), sodium and potassium (fluid balance, nerve conduction), zinc, copper, magnesium (enzymes). Water: 75 per cent of an infant's and 60 per cent of an adult's body; transport, digestion, excretion, temperature regulation and solvent. Roughage (cellulose in fruits and vegetables): bowel movement, prevents constipation, retains water, helps control blood sugar and cholesterol.

Daily energy needs depend on age, sex, occupation, pregnancy and lactation: infants 100-120 kcal per kg; children 1200-2000; adolescent boys 2500 and girls 2200; adult man sedentary 2400, moderate work 2800, heavy work 4000; woman 2400; pregnant woman (later half) 3300; lactating mother 3700. A balanced diet contains all the nutrients in the right proportion; a pregnant woman needs a special diet rich in proteins, iron, calcium, folic acid, vitamins and energy for the growth of the foetus and her own health.

Protein energy malnutrition (PEM): kwashiorkor (protein deficiency in a child whose diet is mostly carbohydrate; swollen belly, oedema, thin limbs, skin and hair changes) and marasmus (deficiency of both calories and proteins; severe wasting with thin limbs, an old-man look and a prominent ribcage). Causes of PEM: poverty and poor diet, early weaning, infections and ignorance. Obesity: excess fat deposition due to overeating and lack of exercise; predisposes to hypertension, atherosclerosis, heart attack and diabetes; prevented by a balanced diet and exercise. Hypervitaminosis: excess intake of vitamins, especially fat-soluble A and D, causes harmful effects such as bone and liver damage.
